doc.title: James Lincoln Collier interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 14, 2007

title: Joining ELS via jazz records; Hamilton's black quota and fraternity bans
summary: A cousin showed him 78 jazz records and brought him into ELS; he adds that Hamilton took one black student per class and many fraternities barred Jews.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up under segregation: schools, neighborhoods, Jim Crow

blocks.x: those sorts of things that always looked good to fraternity people. But I was a left wing guy. I wasn’t going to send this paper in. So I never — the fraternities just didn’t even know I existed, which is what I wanted. I mean I didn’t want to have anything to do with that, which I didn’t know anything about fraternities, but I just assumed they must be bad. And they were in a lot of ways. But I got up there and it turned out I had a cousin who I didn’t know, in fact had never heard of, but somebody told me you have your cousin up there, and he was one of these older guys who had been in combat. And he had been told off by his parents, “Now you have to go over and look up Jim Collier, your young cousin.” So he came and got me and he invited me over to the ELS house, which was then it was an independent house. It didn’t have any national affiliation. But it was basically a fraternity like any of the rest of them, although we did try to keep out grades up, I mean there was some point to that. And so he was showing me around the house, “Would you like to see our rooms” and so he took me into his room and here’s all this array of 78 jazz records. Here’s Bix Beiderbecke, here’s the Billy Banks Rhythm Makers, here’s Louis Armstrong, here’s Bessie Smith. And my eyes popped open because when I went to high school I was the only kid in high school who knew anything about jazz. And so — well not quite, but I mean you know — and, “You guys like this stuff?” And he ran down the hall and got a couple of his buddies and they came over and the next thing I know I’m listening to records with these guys. And so that was a done deal. So then they asked me to join ELS and I did. So that was — so to me there was sort of a jazz component to that. I think there’s something — I think I ought to tell you, this is another thing that’s not quite apropos to what we were talking about, but I think this ought to be on record. This is an important story. When my class had its fiftieth reunion I wrote to, I’ve forgotten who it was the class annalist, somebody there who writes the annals, whatever, and I said this is a story that you really ought to focus on. At that time Hamilton was admitting one black per class. And that is correct. And in my class there was a boy/man, whatever you want to say, student called Ace Lawrence, out of a class of 150, one black, and he was immediately elected president of the class. Nobody knew anything about him but that was the way it was. And somebody taxed the administration office about that and was told no, no, we would be glad to take two or three blacks if we could find them. Now that was the situation. With Jews it was different. Jews, there were quite a number of Jews, and ELS house, which had no national affiliation, we could take whoever we wanted and we did have Jewish kids in our fraternity, that was not an issue. But many of the fraternities had clauses in their charters which said they could not take Jews. That was spelled out. They had to be Christians. Everyone had to be Christians.
